header: Kasr Al Ainy 205 NEU · CNS physiology (synaptic transmission, neuronal pools, sensory receptors, pain pathways, ascending tracts and muscle spindles) — authored from the 205 NEU EOM 2024 exam paper (batch code 197, printed date 28/11/2024), continuing the same paper as the 2024-eom-cns-gross-anatomy cluster (Q29-52); this cluster is Q53-75. Keys read from green-highlight answer markings, confirmed by rendering pages 8-10 at 170dpi and reading every highlight by eye. Department books for this module (Physiology CNS/general, image-only, no text layer) were not OCR'd; explanations are grounded in standard neurophysiology consistent with the paper's own render-confirmed key. Q72 note: the exam key wording says tabes dorsalis is due to 'virus' infection, but the causative organism is the spirochaete Treponema pallidum (neurosyphilis); option a is keyed for its correct localisation to the posterior root ganglia, and the explanation states the accurate aetiology.

questions.title: Characteristic of presynaptic inhibition
questions.question: Presynaptic inhibition is characterized by:

options.A: Decreased Cl- influx into presynaptic terminals
options.B: Hyperpolarization of presynaptic terminals
options.C: Increased Ca2+ influx into post-synaptic neuron
options.D: A 3rd neuron secreting serotonin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Presynaptic inhibition is associated with an INCREASE in Cl- (and K+) conductance at the presynaptic terminal, not a decrease in Cl- influx.
explanations.B: Correct. Presynaptic inhibition acts through an axo-axonic synapse in which an inhibitory (usually GABAergic) interneuron hyperpolarises/less-depolarises the presynaptic terminal of an excitatory neuron. This reduces opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels when the action potential arrives, so less transmitter is released. The effect selectively damps that one input without altering the postsynaptic cell's overall excitability, which is what distinguishes it from postsynaptic inhibition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased Ca2+ entry would ENHANCE transmitter release; and the Ca2+ change in presynaptic inhibition is at the presynaptic terminal, not the postsynaptic neuron.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A third serotonergic neuron is not the mechanism of presynaptic inhibition; presynaptic inhibition is mediated by a GABAergic axo-axonic synapse reducing presynaptic Ca2+ entry.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperpolarisation of the presynaptic terminal (reducing Ca2+ entry and transmitter release) as the mechanism of presynaptic inhibition.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Synaptic Transmission > Presynaptic Inhibition

questions.title: Property of synaptic transmission
questions.question: Concerning synaptic transmission:

options.A: Depends on presence of voltage-gated Ca 2+ channels in the postsynaptic membrane
options.B: Presynaptic knobs release only an excitatory transmitter
options.C: It is physiologically terminated by block of postsynaptic receptors
options.D: It is inhibited by hypoglycemia and acidosis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The voltage-gated Ca2+ channels that trigger release are in the PREsynaptic membrane, not the postsynaptic membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Presynaptic terminals can release excitatory OR inhibitory transmitters (e.g. glutamate vs GABA/glycine), depending on the neuron.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transmission is terminated physiologically by removal of transmitter from the cleft (reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, diffusion), not by blocking postsynaptic receptors.
explanations.D: Correct. Synaptic transmission is the most metabolically demanding and chemically sensitive step in a neural pathway, because transmitter synthesis, vesicle recycling and ion pumping are energy-dependent. It is therefore readily depressed by hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and acidosis, whereas alkalosis tends to increase excitability. This metabolic vulnerability at the synapse is why such disturbances rapidly impair CNS function and consciousness.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise hypoglycaemia and acidosis as depressants of synaptic transmission, and place the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels presynaptically.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Synaptic Transmission > Special Properties

questions.title: Requirement for CNS neurotransmitter release
questions.question: The release of neurotransmitter at a chemical synapse in the CNS is dependent on:

options.A: Synthesis of acetylcholinesterase
options.B: Hyperpolarization of the synaptic terminal
options.C: Opening of ligand-gated calcium channel
options.D: Influx of calcium into the presynaptic terminal

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholinesterase degrades acetylcholine to TERMINATE its action; it is not required to release transmitter (and most CNS synapses are not cholinergic).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Release requires DEPOLARISATION of the terminal to open Ca2+ channels; hyperpolarisation reduces release.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Ca2+ channels that trigger release are VOLTAGE-gated, opened by the depolarisation of the arriving action potential, not ligand-gated.
explanations.D: Correct. When the action potential depolarises the presynaptic terminal it opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and the resulting Ca2+ influx triggers vesicle fusion and exocytosis of transmitter into the cleft. Release is graded with Ca2+ entry and is abolished if extracellular Ca2+ is removed or the channels are blocked. This makes presynaptic Ca2+ influx the essential, rate-limiting trigger for chemical transmission.

questions.learning_objective: State that neurotransmitter release depends on Ca2+ influx into the presynaptic terminal through voltage-gated channels.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Synaptic Transmission > Transmitter Release

questions.title: Nature of the inhibitory postsynaptic potential
questions.question: Inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSPs):

options.A: Interacts with other potentials to move the membrane potential of postsynaptic neuron away or toward firing level
options.B: Is produced by decreased Cl- conductance
options.C: Can be produced by an increase in Na+ conductance
options.D: Is produced as a result of the presence of an inhibitory 3rd neuron

explanations.A: Correct. An IPSP is a graded hyperpolarising potential that summates algebraically with excitatory inputs (EPSPs) on the postsynaptic neuron. Through this interaction it shifts the membrane potential relative to the firing threshold — moving it away from threshold (or opposing movement toward it) — so the cell fires only if the net effect still reaches threshold. This integrative interaction of postsynaptic potentials is the essence of how a neuron decides to fire.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The IPSP is produced by INCREASED Cl- conductance (or increased K+ conductance), not decreased Cl- conductance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased Na+ conductance is DEPOLARISING and produces an EPSP, not an inhibitory (hyperpolarising) potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The IPSP is a postsynaptic event generated by inhibitory transmitter on the neuron's own membrane; it does not require a separate 'third neuron' (that description confuses it with pathway-level inhibitory circuits).

questions.learning_objective: Describe the IPSP as a hyperpolarising postsynaptic potential (increased Cl-/K+ conductance) that summates with other inputs relative to threshold.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Synaptic Transmission > Postsynaptic Potentials

questions.title: Mechanism of post-tetanic potentiation
questions.question: Post-tetanic potentiation in synapses:

options.A: Is due to activation of AMPA and NMDA receptors by glutamate
options.B: Is produced by an excitatory 3rd neuron secreting serotonin
options.C: Is due to opening of transmitter gated Cl- channels
options.D: Is due to accumulation of calcium in the presynaptic terminal

explanations.A: Incorrect. AMPA/NMDA receptor activation underlies long-term potentiation (a postsynaptic mechanism), which is distinct from post-tetanic potentiation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A serotonergic 'third neuron' is not the mechanism; post-tetanic potentiation is intrinsic to the stimulated presynaptic terminal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Opening transmitter-gated Cl- channels is an inhibitory (IPSP) event, not the cause of potentiation.
explanations.D: Correct. After a rapid train (tetanus) of presynaptic stimuli, Ca2+ enters the terminal faster than it can be pumped out, so residual Ca2+ accumulates in the presynaptic terminal. Subsequent single stimuli then release more transmitter, producing larger postsynaptic responses for seconds to minutes. This makes post-tetanic potentiation a presynaptic form of short-term synaptic plasticity.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute post-tetanic potentiation to residual presynaptic Ca2+ accumulation after high-frequency stimulation.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Synaptic Transmission > Synaptic Plasticity

questions.title: Function of convergence in a neuronal pool
questions.question: Convergence in a neuronal pool:

options.A: Is the state when one neuron stimulates many neurons
options.B: Helps in the distribution of signals
options.C: Helps in the selection of important signals and ignoring unimportant ones
options.D: Involves temporal summation of a weak input fiber along sensory pathways

explanations.A: Incorrect. One neuron stimulating many describes DIVERGENCE, the opposite of convergence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Distribution of signals is the role of divergence (amplifying/spreading), not convergence.
explanations.C: Correct. Convergence is the arrangement in which many presynaptic fibres terminate on a single postsynaptic neuron. By allowing that neuron to integrate inputs from multiple sources through spatial summation, convergence lets the pool select important signals and ignore unimportant ones. This integrative, decision-making role is the functional significance of convergence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes summation along a pathway rather than the many-onto-one anatomical arrangement that defines convergence.

questions.learning_objective: Define convergence as many inputs onto one neuron enabling integration and selection of important signals.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Neuronal Pools > Convergence

questions.title: Basis of facilitation in a neuronal pool
questions.question: Facilitation:

options.A: Is due to stimulation of 2 input neurons away from each other
options.B: Is due to stimulation of 2 input neurons close to each other
options.C: Number of action potentials released is less than if each input neuron is stimulated alone
options.D: Occurs when the two afferent neurons have a common discharge zone

explanations.A: Correct. Each input fibre has a central discharge (liminal) zone surrounded by a facilitated subliminal fringe of neurons brought only part-way to threshold. When two input fibres are stimulated far enough APART that their discharge zones do not overlap but their subliminal fringes do, the subthreshold potentials summate and extra fringe neurons now reach threshold, so the combined response exceeds the sum of the separate responses. That supra-additive gain from overlapping fringes is facilitation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inputs close together have overlapping DISCHARGE zones, which gives occlusion (a sub-additive response), not facilitation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fewer impulses than the sum of the separate responses describes OCCLUSION, the opposite of facilitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A common (shared) discharge zone underlies occlusion; facilitation depends on overlap of the subliminal fringes of spaced inputs.

questions.learning_objective: Explain facilitation as overlap of the subliminal fringes of two spaced inputs, contrasting it with occlusion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Neuronal Pools > Facilitation and Occlusion

questions.title: Property of the receptor potential
questions.question: The receptor potential:

options.A: Has a long absolute refractory period
options.B: Amplitude is not related to the strength of the stimulus
options.C: Always generates an action potential in the receptor
options.D: Its duration is longer than action potential duration

explanations.A: Incorrect. A long absolute refractory period is a property of the action potential; the receptor potential is a graded local potential without this refractory behaviour.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The receptor potential is GRADED — its amplitude increases with stimulus strength.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The receptor potential triggers action potentials only if it reaches threshold; a subthreshold receptor potential fires no spike.
explanations.D: Correct. The receptor (generator) potential is a local, non-propagated, graded depolarisation whose time course is longer than that of the action potential it may trigger. Because it outlasts the brief all-or-none spike, a maintained stimulus can drive repetitive firing during the receptor potential. This longer duration and graded, non-propagated nature distinguish it from the action potential.

questions.learning_objective: State that the receptor potential is graded and non-propagated, with a duration that outlasts the action potential.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Sensory Receptors > Receptor Potential

questions.title: Regarding sensory receptors
questions.question: Regarding sensory receptors:

options.A: Stimulus energy is converted into a local depolarization
options.B: The receptor potential is graded and self-propagating
options.C: The receptor potential can be produced by only one form of energy
options.D: The frequency of action potentials generated doubles when the strength of the stimulus doubles

explanations.A: Correct. A sensory receptor transduces its adequate stimulus into a local graded depolarisation — the receptor potential — by opening ion channels in the receptor membrane. This conversion of stimulus energy into a local electrical change is the defining event of sensory transduction, occurring before any action potentials are generated. The receptor potential then spreads electrotonically to the spike-initiating zone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The receptor potential is graded but NOT self-propagating; it spreads passively (electrotonically), unlike the self-propagating action potential.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A receptor is most sensitive (low threshold) to its adequate stimulus, but strong energy of ANOTHER form can also excite it, so it is not limited to only one energy form.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Impulse frequency rises with stimulus strength but follows a power/logarithmic function, not a simple linear doubling.

questions.learning_objective: Describe sensory transduction as conversion of stimulus energy into a local graded depolarisation.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Sensory Receptors > Transduction

questions.title: How receptors code increased stimulus intensity
questions.question: Receptors detect increased stimulus intensity by:

options.A: Lowering the threshold for receptor stimulation
options.B: By generating receptor potentials having higher magnitudes
options.C: By generating nerve impulses that are transmitted along sensory fibers at higher velocities
options.D: By enhancing the central effects of sensory impulses

explanations.A: Incorrect. Threshold is a fixed property of the receptor; intensity is not signalled by lowering it.
explanations.B: Correct. A stronger stimulus produces a receptor potential of greater magnitude, which in turn raises the frequency of action potentials in the sensory fibre (frequency coding) and recruits more receptors (population coding). The larger-amplitude receptor potential is the receptor-level event that encodes increased intensity. Thus intensity is coded by receptor-potential amplitude and impulse frequency, not by any change in conduction speed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conduction velocity is fixed by fibre diameter and myelination and does not change with stimulus strength.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Central 'enhancement' is not how the receptor itself signals intensity; the receptor encodes intensity peripherally by receptor-potential amplitude and firing frequency.

questions.learning_objective: Identify larger-magnitude receptor potentials (and higher firing frequency) as the code for increased stimulus intensity.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Sensory Receptors > Stimulus Intensity Coding

questions.title: Basis of stimulus localisation
questions.question: The ability to localize the site of stimuli depends upon:

options.A: The type of the stimulated receptor
options.B: The rate of adaptation of the stimulated receptors
options.C: Connections between the receptor and the sensory cortex
options.D: The nature of the stimulus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Receptor type encodes modality, not the spatial site of the stimulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adaptation rate encodes whether a receptor signals change or steady state, not location.
explanations.C: Correct. Localisation depends on the specific point-to-point ('labelled line') connection between a given receptor and a discrete point in the sensory cortex, preserved by the somatotopic organisation of the pathway. Because each body region projects to its own cortical locus, activity arriving there is referred back to the corresponding body part. Localisation is therefore a property of the wiring, and two-point discrimination is finest where this projection is densest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nature (modality) of the stimulus is what it is, not where it is; it does not determine localisation.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute stimulus localisation to labelled-line receptor-to-cortex connections.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Sensory Receptors > Sensory Localisation

questions.title: Adaptation class of thermal receptors
questions.question: Thermal receptors are:

options.A: Rapidly adapting receptors
options.B: Moderately adapting receptors
options.C: Are stimulated at zero0 C
options.D: All are encapsulated receptors

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rapidly adapting receptors (e.g. Pacinian corpuscles) fire only at stimulus onset/offset; thermoreceptors are not rapidly adapting.
explanations.B: Correct. Thermal (cold and warm) receptors are moderately/partially adapting free nerve endings: they discharge strongly when temperature changes, then settle to a lower steady rate that still signals the maintained temperature. This partial adaptation lets them report both the change and the ongoing thermal level. They are not rapidly adapting like Pacinian corpuscles nor non-adapting like nociceptors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thermoreceptors operate over physiological temperature ranges; they are not specifically 'stimulated at 0 C' (near-freezing cold can even cause paradoxical or pain responses).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thermoreceptors are free (non-encapsulated) nerve endings, not encapsulated receptors.

questions.learning_objective: Classify thermoreceptors as moderately adapting free nerve endings.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Sensory Receptors > Thermoreceptors

questions.title: Properties of pain receptors
questions.question: Pain receptors are:

options.A: Similar in structure to paccinian corpuscles
options.B: Sensitized by a rise in the local tissue K+ concentration
options.C: Quick to adapt to a constant stimulus
options.D: Stimulated in the wall of the GIT by sharp cutting

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nociceptors are free (bare) nerve endings, structurally unlike the encapsulated, laminated Pacinian corpuscle.
explanations.B: Correct. Pain receptors are free nerve endings sensitised and activated by chemical mediators released from damaged tissue — a rise in local tissue K+ concentration is a key one, along with H+, bradykinin, prostaglandins, serotonin and histamine. This chemical sensitisation lowers their threshold and sustains firing while injury persists. Their identity as chemically sensitised free endings is central to inflammatory hyperalgesia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nociceptors adapt very little or not at all, so pain persists while the noxious stimulus continues (protective).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The gut wall is insensitive to sharp cutting or burning; visceral nociceptors respond instead to ischaemia, spasm and over-distension.

questions.learning_objective: Describe nociceptors as non-adapting free nerve endings sensitised by raised local tissue K+.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Pain > Nociceptors

questions.title: Features of visceral pain
questions.question: Visceral pain:

options.A: Is poorly localized compared with pain arising in skin
options.B: May cause reflex contraction of overlying skeletal muscle
options.C: May cause reflex vomiting
options.D: All of the above

explanations.A: Incorrect only as a sole answer. Visceral pain IS poorly localised (sparse afferents, convergence with somatic inputs), but this is not the only true statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect only as a sole answer. Visceral pain CAN cause reflex guarding/rigidity of the overlying skeletal muscle through viscero-somatic reflexes, but other statements are also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect only as a sole answer. Visceral pain CAN provoke reflex autonomic effects such as vomiting, sweating and bradycardia, but this too is not the only correct statement.
explanations.D: Correct. All three features are characteristic of visceral pain: it is poorly localised compared with somatic (skin) pain, it can cause reflex contraction (guarding) of the overlying skeletal muscle, and it can trigger reflex autonomic effects such as vomiting. Because each individual statement is true, 'all of the above' is the correct single answer.

questions.learning_objective: List the features of visceral pain: poor localisation, reflex overlying-muscle spasm and reflex autonomic effects.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Pain > Visceral Pain

questions.title: Fibres mediating tactile inhibition of pain
questions.question: Inhibition of pain signals by tactile stimulation of a skin surface involves:

options.A: Type A alpha fibers in peripheral nerves
options.B: Type A beta fibers in peripheral nerves
options.C: Type A delta fibers in peripheral nerves
options.D: Type C fibers in peripheral nerves

explanations.A: Incorrect. Type A-alpha fibres are the largest motor/proprioceptive fibres, not the tactile afferents that gate pain.
explanations.B: Correct. According to the gate-control theory, activity in large myelinated tactile afferents — type A-beta fibres — from a skin surface excites inhibitory circuits in the dorsal horn that 'close the gate' on incoming pain signals. This reduces transmission of the A-delta and C fibre pain pathway to the brain, which is why rubbing, massage or TENS around an injury relieves pain. The inhibiting fibres are therefore the A-beta tactile fibres.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type A-delta fibres CARRY fast, sharp pain; they are part of the pain pathway being inhibited, not the tactile inhibitor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Type C fibres carry slow, burning pain; like A-delta they are the pain-transmitting fibres, not the tactile fibres that close the gate.

questions.learning_objective: Identify A-beta tactile fibres as the input that inhibits pain transmission in the gate-control mechanism.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Pain > Gate Control

questions.title: Tract interrupted by anterolateral cordotomy
questions.question: After anterolateral cordotomy, relief of pain is due to interruption of:

options.A: Dorsal column
options.B: Ventral spinothalamic tract
options.C: Ventral spinocerebellar tract
options.D: Lateral spinothalamic tract

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal column carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception, not pain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ventral (anterior) spinothalamic tract carries crude touch and pressure, not the sharp pain relieved by cordotomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum, not pain.
explanations.D: Correct. The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature from the contralateral half of the body, its fibres having crossed within one or two segments of entering the cord. Anterolateral cordotomy divides this tract in the anterolateral quadrant, abolishing pain and temperature on the opposite side below the lesion. This is exactly why the operation relieves otherwise intractable pain.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute pain relief after anterolateral cordotomy to interruption of the lateral spinothalamic tract.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Ascending Pathways > Spinothalamic Tract

questions.title: Serotonergic neurons of the supraspinal analgesia system
questions.question: The neurons that release serotonin as chemical transmitter are located in which part of the supraspinal analgesia system:

options.A: Periaqueductal gray area
options.B: Interneurons of the spinal cord
options.C: Periventricular area
options.D: Nucleus raphe magnus

explanations.A: Incorrect. The periaqueductal grey is the upstream tier that excites the raphe magnus; its neurons are not the serotonergic ones in this scheme.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dorsal-horn (cord) interneurons of this system release enkephalin, not serotonin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The periventricular area (with the periaqueductal grey) is an upstream analgesia centre, not the serotonin-secreting nucleus.
explanations.D: Correct. In the endogenous analgesia system the nucleus raphe magnus (lower pons/upper medulla) contains the serotonin-releasing neurons. Excited by the periaqueductal grey, their axons descend to the dorsal horn where serotonin drives local enkephalin interneurons to inhibit incoming C and A-delta pain fibres. Thus the serotonergic neurons of this pathway are located in the nucleus raphe magnus.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the serotonin-releasing neurons of the descending analgesia system in the nucleus raphe magnus.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Pain > Descending Analgesia System

questions.title: Deficit from a dorsal column lesion
questions.question: A lesion of the dorsal column pathway is most likely to affect:

options.A: Fine touch
options.B: Hearing
options.C: Pain sensation
options.D: Temperature sensation

explanations.A: Correct. The dorsal column–medial lemniscus system carries fine (two-point discriminative) touch, vibration and conscious proprioception, so its lesion most affects fine touch (with vibration and joint-position sense, a positive Romberg and sensory ataxia). Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract and are relatively spared. Hence fine touch is the modality lost.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hearing is carried by the auditory pathway, unrelated to the dorsal columns.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pain is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Temperature is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dorsal column pathway subserves fine touch, vibration and proprioception, sparing pain and temperature.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Ascending Pathways > Dorsal Column

questions.title: Sensory findings in spinal cord hemisection
questions.question: A subject who suffers from right hemisection of the spinal cord shows:

options.A: Upper motor neuron paralysis at the level of the hemisection
options.B: Loss of pain and temperature on the right side below the level of the section
options.C: Loss of fine touch and vibration sense on the left side below the level of the section
options.D: Loss of all sensations on the same side at the level of the section

explanations.A: Incorrect. At the level of the lesion the segmental motor loss is LOWER motor neuron (destroyed anterior horn/roots of that segment); upper-motor-neuron (spastic) paralysis appears BELOW the lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pain and temperature loss is CONTRALATERAL (left side) below the lesion, because the spinothalamic tract has crossed — not ipsilateral (right).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fine touch and vibration loss is IPSILATERAL (right side, same as the lesion) below the level, because the dorsal columns ascend uncrossed — not on the left.
explanations.D: Correct. At the actual level of the section, destruction of the dorsal root and all entering fibres of that segment causes loss of ALL sensory modalities on the same (ipsilateral) side in that segmental band. Below the lesion the deficits dissociate — ipsilateral dorsal-column and motor loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss — but the 'all sensations, same side, at the level' statement is the correct one here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that at the level of a cord hemisection all sensations are lost ipsilaterally, with dissociated deficits below the lesion.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Spinal Cord > Brown-Séquard Syndrome

questions.title: Nature of tabes dorsalis
questions.question: Tabes dorsalis is:

options.A: Due to virus infection of the posterior root ganglia
options.B: Accompanied with shuffling gait
options.C: Accompanied with incoordination of voluntary movements
options.D: Accompanied with loss of crude touch

explanations.A: Correct (per the exam key, for its localisation). Tabes dorsalis is degeneration centred on the posterior (dorsal) roots and their ganglia and the dorsal columns, producing sensory ataxia. Note that the true cause is the spirochaete Treponema pallidum (late neurosyphilis), NOT a virus — the option's wording is inaccurate on aetiology, but among the four choices only this one correctly localises the lesion to the posterior root ganglia. The other options describe conditions that are not tabes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A shuffling gait is characteristic of Parkinsonism; tabes causes a high-stepping, stamping sensory-ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Incoordination of voluntary movements (intention tremor, dysmetria) is cerebellar; the incoordination in tabes is sensory ataxia from proprioceptive loss, worse with eyes closed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tabes damages the dorsal columns, so fine touch, vibration and proprioception are lost; crude touch (spinothalamic) is relatively preserved.

questions.learning_objective: Localise tabes dorsalis to posterior root/dorsal column degeneration (a neurosyphilitic, not viral, process) causing sensory ataxia.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Spinal Cord > Tabes Dorsalis

field_notes.keyCaveat: exam option a says 'virus'; true cause is Treponema pallidum (neurosyphilis) — keyed for its correct localisation to the posterior root ganglia; explanation states accurate aetiology.

questions.title: Regarding muscle spindles
questions.question: Regarding muscle spindles:

options.A: Are composed of extrafusal fibers
options.B: Gamma efferents supply their peripheral parts
options.C: Nuclear chain fibers show dynamic response
options.D: Afferent discharge decreased with muscle stretch

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscle spindles are composed of small INTRAFUSAL fibres; the large force-generating fibres outside the spindle are the extrafusal fibres.
explanations.B: Correct. Each intrafusal fibre has a central sensory (equatorial) region and contractile polar ends; the polar ends are supplied by gamma (fusimotor) efferents. Gamma activation shortens the poles and keeps the central sensory region taut, resetting spindle sensitivity as the whole muscle shortens. This gamma supply to the peripheral (polar) parts is a defining feature of the spindle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dynamic response is a property of nuclear-BAG fibres (via the primary ending); nuclear-chain fibres give a more static response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Afferent discharge from the spindle INCREASES with muscle stretch (the spindle is a stretch receptor), not decreases.

questions.learning_objective: State that the spindle's intrafusal polar regions are supplied by gamma efferents, keeping the sensory region responsive.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Control > Muscle Spindle

questions.title: Afferent of the nuclear-bag central region
questions.question: The central receptor area of nuclear-bag fibers is innervated by:

options.A: A gamma nerve fibers
options.B: A beta nerve fibers
options.C: An alpha nerve fibers
options.D: Ia nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. A-gamma fibres are EFFERENT (fusimotor) to the polar contractile ends, not the central sensory afferent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A-beta fibres are cutaneous tactile afferents, not the central spindle ending.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A-alpha (efferent) fibres innervate extrafusal muscle fibres via the motor end plate, not the spindle's sensory region.
explanations.D: Correct. The central (equatorial) region of the nuclear-bag fibre carries the primary (annulospiral) ending, which is served by large, fast type Ia afferent fibres. These Ia fibres signal both the rate of change of length (dynamic) and static length. The secondary (flower-spray) ending on nuclear-chain fibres is served by type II fibres, but the central nuclear-bag receptor is a group Ia afferent.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the primary (annulospiral) ending of the nuclear-bag fibre's central region as innervated by type Ia afferents.
questions.module_subject: 205 NEU > Physiology > Motor Control > Spindle Afferents

questions.title: Response elicited by spindle Ia afferents on sudden stretch
questions.question: When a muscle is suddenly stretched, a signal is transmitted over Ia sensory fibers from muscle spindles. Which of the following statements best describes the response elicited by these spindle afferent signals?

options.A: Contraction of the muscle in which the active spindles are located
options.B: Relaxation of the muscle in which the active spindles are located
options.C: Relaxation of intrafusal fibers in the active spindles
options.D: Direct synaptic activation of gamma motor neurons

explanations.A: Correct. The stretch (myotatic) reflex is monosynaptic: sudden stretch excites the spindle primary endings, whose Ia afferents synapse directly on the alpha motor neurons of the SAME (homonymous) muscle, causing it to contract and oppose the stretch (e.g. the knee jerk). This resists lengthening and maintains muscle tone and posture. Hence Ia activity produces contraction of the muscle containing the active spindles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stretched muscle CONTRACTS, not relaxes; relaxation would not oppose the stretch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intrafusal fibres are controlled by gamma efferents; the Ia stretch signal does not relax them, and this is not the reflex output.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ia afferents act on ALPHA motor neurons (monosynaptically) to contract the muscle; they do not directly drive gamma motor neurons.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the monosynaptic stretch reflex: spindle Ia afferents contract the homonymous muscle via alpha motor neurons.
